response.text:
## Parameter space

The probabilities are nonnegative iff

\[
0\le \theta \le 1.
\]

For likelihood differentiation and standard asymptotics below, take the true value in the interior \((0,1)\).

Let

\[
A=y_2+y_3.
\]

For the observed data,

\[
p(y;\theta)\propto (1+\theta)^{y_1}(1-\theta)^A\theta^{y_4}.
\]

---

# (i) EM algorithm from the augmentation

The complete data are

\[
Z=(u_1,u_2,y_2,y_3,y_4),\qquad y_1=u_1+u_2,
\]

with

\[
Z\sim \text{Multinomial}\left(n;\frac13,\frac{\theta}{3},\frac{1-\theta}{3},\frac{1-\theta}{3},\frac{\theta}{3}\right).
\]

The complete-data log-likelihood, dropping terms not involving \(\theta\), is

\[
\ell_c(\theta;Z)
= (u_2+y_4)\log\theta + (y_2+y_3)\log(1-\theta).
\]

Given \(Y\), only \(u_2\) is missing. Conditional on \(y_1=u_1+u_2\),

\[
U_2\mid Y,\theta \sim \text{Binomial}\left(y_1,\frac{\theta}{1+\theta}\right).
\]

Thus at iteration \(t\), with current value \(\theta^{(t)}\),

\[
m^{(t)}
:=\mathbb E_{\theta^{(t)}}[U_2\mid Y]
= y_1\frac{\theta^{(t)}}{1+\theta^{(t)}}.
\]

The EM \(Q\)-function is, up to constants,

\[
Q(\theta\mid \theta^{(t)})
=
(m^{(t)}+y_4)\log\theta
+
A\log(1-\theta).
\]

Maximizing gives

\[
\frac{m^{(t)}+y_4}{\theta}
-
\frac{A}{1-\theta}
=0,
\]

so the EM update is

\[
\boxed{
\theta^{(t+1)}
=
\frac{m^{(t)}+y_4}{m^{(t)}+y_4+A}
=
\frac{y_1\theta^{(t)}/(1+\theta^{(t)})+y_4}
{y_1\theta^{(t)}/(1+\theta^{(t)})+y_4+y_2+y_3}.
}
\]

Because the observed log-likelihood is strictly concave on \((0,1)\) when the relevant counts are positive, the EM sequence converges to the unique MLE.

For reference, the observed score is

\[
\ell'(\theta)
=
\frac{y_1}{1+\theta}
-
\frac{A}{1-\theta}
+
\frac{y_4}{\theta}.
\]

Setting this equal to zero gives

\[
y_4+(y_1-A)\theta-n\theta^2=0,
\]

so the interior MLE is also

\[
\boxed{
\hat\theta
=
\frac{(y_1-A)+\sqrt{(y_1-A)^2+4ny_4}}{2n}.
}
\]

---

# (ii) Louis identity for the observed second derivative

Let \(f(z;\theta)\) be the complete-data pmf and \(p(y;\theta)\) the observed-data pmf. For fixed \(Y=y\), let

\[
h_\theta(z\mid y)
=
\frac{f(z;\theta)}{p(y;\theta)}
\]

be the conditional pmf of \(Z\mid Y=y\).

Define the complete-data score and Hessian by

\[
S_c(Z;\theta)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log f(Z;\theta),
\qquad
H_c(Z;\theta)=\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log f(Z;\theta).
\]

The observed score is

\[
S_o(Y;\theta)
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p(Y;\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y].
\]

Indeed,

\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p(Y;\theta)
=
\frac{1}{p(Y;\theta)}
\sum_{z:z\mapsto Y}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}f(z;\theta)
=
\sum_{z:z\mapsto Y} h_\theta(z\mid Y) S_c(z;\theta).
\]

Differentiate again. Since

\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}h_\theta(z\mid Y)
=
h_\theta(z\mid Y)\{S_c(z;\theta)-S_o(Y;\theta)\},
\]

we get

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log p(Y;\theta)
&=
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}
\mathbb E_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y] \\
&=
\mathbb E_\theta[H_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
+
\mathbb E_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)^2\mid Y]
-
\{\mathbb E_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]\}^2 \\
&=
\mathbb E_\theta[H_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
+
\operatorname{Var}_\theta\{S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}\log p(Y;\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta\left[
\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}\log f(Z;\theta)\mid Y
\right]
+
\operatorname{Var}_\theta\left[
\frac{d}{d\theta}\log f(Z;\theta)\mid Y
\right].
}
\]

This is the scalar version of Louis’ missing information identity.

---

# (iii) Observed Fisher information from the EM output

From the complete-data log-likelihood,

\[
\ell_c(\theta;Z)
=
(U_2+y_4)\log\theta + A\log(1-\theta),
\]

the complete-data score is

\[
S_c(Z;\theta)
=
\frac{U_2+y_4}{\theta}
-
\frac{A}{1-\theta},
\]

and the complete-data second derivative is

\[
H_c(Z;\theta)
=
-\frac{U_2+y_4}{\theta^2}
-
\frac{A}{(1-\theta)^2}.
\]

Under \(Z\mid Y,\theta\),

\[
U_2\mid Y,\theta
\sim \text{Binomial}\left(y_1,\frac{\theta}{1+\theta}\right).
\]

Let

\[
q(\theta)=\frac{\theta}{1+\theta}.
\]

Then

\[
m(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[U_2\mid Y]=y_1q(\theta),
\]

and

\[
v(\theta):=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U_2\mid Y)
=
y_1q(\theta)\{1-q(\theta)\}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[H_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
=
-\frac{m(\theta)+y_4}{\theta^2}
-
\frac{A}{(1-\theta)^2},
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{Var}_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
=
\frac{v(\theta)}{\theta^2}.
\]

By part (ii),

\[
\ell''(\theta)
=
-\frac{m(\theta)+y_4}{\theta^2}
-
\frac{A}{(1-\theta)^2}
+
\frac{v(\theta)}{\theta^2}.
\]

Thus the observed Fisher information is

\[
J_{\text{obs}}(\theta)
=
-\ell''(\theta)
=
\frac{m(\theta)+y_4}{\theta^2}
+
\frac{A}{(1-\theta)^2}
-
\frac{v(\theta)}{\theta^2}.
\]

At the EM limit \(\hat\theta\), the EM output gives \(m(\hat\theta)\), and \(v(\hat\theta)\) is obtained from the same conditional binomial distribution. Hence

\[
\boxed{
\widehat J_{\text{obs}}
=
\frac{m(\hat\theta)+y_4}{\hat\theta^2}
+
\frac{A}{(1-\hat\theta)^2}
-
\frac{v(\hat\theta)}{\hat\theta^2}.
}
\]

Equivalently, simplifying,

\[
\boxed{
\widehat J_{\text{obs}}
=
\frac{y_1}{(1+\hat\theta)^2}
+
\frac{y_2+y_3}{(1-\hat\theta)^2}
+
\frac{y_4}{\hat\theta^2}.
}
\]

The estimated asymptotic variance of \(\hat\theta\) is therefore

\[
\boxed{
\hat V
=
\widehat J_{\text{obs}}^{-1}.
}
\]

---

# (iv) R implementation and numerical result for \(Y=(108,31,27,34)\)

Here \(n=200\), \(A=31+27=58\), and \(y_4=34\).

The score equation is

\[
34+(108-58)\theta-200\theta^2=0,
\]

so

\[
\hat\theta
=
\frac{50+\sqrt{50^2+4(200)(34)}}{400}
=
0.5558422.
\]

The observed information at \(\hat\theta\) is

\[
\widehat J_{\text{obs}}
=
\frac{108}{(1+\hat\theta)^2}
+
\frac{58}{(1-\hat\theta)^2}
+
\frac{34}{\hat\theta^2}
=
448.6667.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\hat V=\frac{1}{448.6667}=0.002228826,
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta)=\sqrt{\hat V}=0.0472104.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\hat\theta \pm \text{SE}
=
0.5558 \pm 0.0472.
}
\]

R code:

```r
em.fit <- function(y, theta0 = 0.5, tol = 1e-12, maxit = 10000) {
  y1 <- y[1]
  y2 <- y[2]
  y3 <- y[3]
  y4 <- y[4]
  A  <- y2 + y3
  
  theta <- theta0
  
  for (iter in 1:maxit) {
    theta.old <- theta
    
    # E-step
    m <- y1 * theta.old / (1 + theta.old)
    
    # M-step
    theta <- (m + y4) / (m + y4 + A)
    
    if (abs(theta - theta.old) < tol) break
  }
  
  # Louis observed information
  q <- theta / (1 + theta)
  m <- y1 * q
  v <- y1 * q * (1 - q)
  
  J <- (m + y4) / theta^2 + A / (1 - theta)^2 - v / theta^2
  V <- 1 / J
  se <- sqrt(V)
  
  list(theta = theta, info = J, V = V, se = se, iter = iter)
}

y <- c(108, 31, 27, 34)
em.fit(y)
```

```r
$V

$se
[1] 0.04721044
```

---

# (v) Simulation study

A reasonable simulation design is:

1. Fix \(n=200\).
2. Choose an interior true value, say \(\theta_0=0.5\).
3. Simulate many datasets \(Y^{(b)}\sim\text{Multinomial}(200;p(\theta_0))\).
4. For each dataset compute \(\hat\theta^{(b)}\) and \(\hat V^{(b)}\).
5. Check:
   - Normality of
     \[
     Z_b
     =
     \frac{\hat\theta^{(b)}-\theta_0}{\sqrt{\hat V^{(b)}}}.
     \]
   - Agreement between
     \[
     \operatorname{Var}_{\text{MC}}(\hat\theta)
     \]
     and
     \[
     \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \hat V^{(b)}.
     \]

R code:

```r
mle.closed <- function(Y) {
  n <- rowSums(Y)
  A <- Y[, 2] + Y[, 3]
  D <- Y[, 1] - A
  y4 <- Y[, 4]
  
  theta.hat <- (D + sqrt(D^2 + 4 * n * y4)) / (2 * n)
  theta.hat
}

obs.info <- function(Y, theta.hat) {
  y1 <- Y[, 1]
  A  <- Y[, 2] + Y[, 3]
  y4 <- Y[, 4]
  
  y1 / (1 + theta.hat)^2 +
    A / (1 - theta.hat)^2 +
    y4 / theta.hat^2
}

sim.check <- function(theta0 = 0.5, n = 200, B = 50000, seed = 123) {
  set.seed(seed)
  
  p <- c((1 + theta0) / 3,
         (1 - theta0) / 3,
         (1 - theta0) / 3,
         theta0 / 3)
  
  Y <- t(rmultinom(B, n, p))
  
  theta.hat <- mle.closed(Y)
  J.hat <- obs.info(Y, theta.hat)
  V.hat <- 1 / J.hat
  se.hat <- sqrt(V.hat)
  
  Z <- (theta.hat - theta0) / se.hat
  
  out <- c(
    mean.theta.hat = mean(theta.hat),
    bias = mean(theta.hat) - theta0,
    empirical.sd = sd(theta.hat),
    mean.SE = mean(se.hat),
    sqrt.mean.Vhat = sqrt(mean(V.hat)),
    var.ratio = var(theta.hat) / mean(V.hat),
    coverage.95 = mean(abs(theta.hat - theta0) <= 1.96 * se.hat),
    mean.Z = mean(Z),
    sd.Z = sd(Z),
    q025.Z = quantile(Z, 0.025),
    q500.Z = quantile(Z, 0.500),
    q975.Z = quantile(Z, 0.975)
  )
  
  print(out)
  
  hist(Z, probability = TRUE, breaks = 50,
       main = "Studentized MLE",
       xlab = expression((hat(theta) - theta[0]) / sqrt(hat(V))))
  curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, col = 2, lwd = 2)
  
  qqnorm(Z)
  qqline(Z, col = 2, lwd = 2)
  
  invisible(out)
}

sim.check(theta0 = 0.5, n = 200, B = 50000)
```


\[

\]

being close to \(1\) confirms that \(\hat V\) is a good estimator of the variance of \(\hat\theta\) at \(n=200\).

\{\mathbb E_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]\}^2 \\
&=
\mathbb E_\theta[H_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
+
\operatorname{Var}_\theta\{S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}\log p(Y;\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta\left[
\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}\log f(Z;\theta)\mid Y
\right]
+
\operatorname{Var}_\theta\left[
\frac{d}{d\theta}\log f(Z;\theta)\mid Y
\right].
}
\]

This is the scalar version of Louis’ missing information identity.

---

# (iii) Observed Fisher information from the EM output

From the complete-data log-likelihood,

\[
\ell_c(\theta;Z)
=
(U_2+y_4)\log\theta + A\log(1-\theta),
\]

the complete-data score is

\[
S_c(Z;\theta)
=
\frac{U_2+y_4}{\theta}
-
\frac{A}{1-\theta},
\]

and the complete-data second derivative is

\[
H_c(Z;\theta)
=
-\frac{U_2+y_4}{\theta^2}
-
\frac{A}{(1-\theta)^2}.
\]

Under \(Z\mid Y,\theta\),

\[
U_2\mid Y,\theta
\sim \text{Binomial}\left(y_1,\frac{\theta}{1+\theta}\right).
\]

Let

\[
q(\theta)=\frac{\theta}{1+\theta}.
\]

Then

\[
m(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[U_2\mid Y]=y_1q(\theta),
\]

and

\[
v(\theta):=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U_2\mid Y)
=
y_1q(\theta)\{1-q(\theta)\}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[H_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
=
-\frac{m(\theta)+y_4}{\theta^2}
-
\frac{A}{(1-\theta)^2},
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{Var}_\theta[S_c(Z;\theta)\mid Y]
=
\frac{v(\theta)}{\theta^2}.
\]

By part (ii),

\[
\ell''(\theta)
=
-\frac{m(\theta)+y_4}{\theta^2}
-
\frac{A}{(1-\theta)^2}
+
\frac{v(\theta)}{\theta^2}.
\]

Thus the observed Fisher information is

\[
J_{\text{obs}}(\theta)
=
-\ell''(\theta)
=
\frac{m(\theta)+y_4}{\theta^2}
+
\frac{A}{(1-\theta)^2}
-
\frac{v(\theta)}{\theta^2}.
\]

At the EM limit \(\hat\theta\), the EM output gives \(m(\hat\theta)\), and \(v(\hat\theta)\) is obtained from the same conditional binomial distribution. Hence

\[
\boxed{
\widehat J_{\text{obs}}
=
\frac{m(\hat\theta)+y_4}{\hat\theta^2}
+
\frac{A}{(1-\hat\theta)^2}
-
\frac{v(\hat\theta)}{\hat\theta^2}.
}
\]

Equivalently, simplifying,

\[
\boxed{
\widehat J_{\text{obs}}
=
\frac{y_1}{(1+\hat\theta)^2}
+
\frac{y_2+y_3}{(1-\hat\theta)^2}
+
\frac{y_4}{\hat\theta^2}.
}
\]

The estimated asymptotic variance of \(\hat\theta\) is therefore

\[
\boxed{
\hat V
=
\widehat J_{\text{obs}}^{-1}.
}
\]

---

# (iv) R implementation and numerical result for \(Y=(108,31,27,34)\)

Here \(n=200\), \(A=31+27=58\), and \(y_4=34\).

The score equation is

\[
34+(108-58)\theta-200\theta^2=0,
\]

so

\[
\hat\theta
=
\frac{50+\sqrt{50^2+4(200)(34)}}{400}
=
0.5558422.
\]

The observed information at \(\hat\theta\) is

\[
\widehat J_{\text{obs}}
=
\frac{108}{(1+\hat\theta)^2}
+
\frac{58}{(1-\hat\theta)^2}
+
\frac{34}{\hat\theta^2}
=
448.6667.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\hat V=\frac{1}{448.6667}=0.002228826,
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta)=\sqrt{\hat V}=0.0472104.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\hat\theta \pm \text{SE}
=
0.5558 \pm 0.0472.
}
\]

R code:

```r
em.fit <- function(y, theta0 = 0.5, tol = 1e-12, maxit = 10000) {
  y1 <- y[1]
  y2 <- y[2]
  y3 <- y[3]
  y4 <- y[4]
  A  <- y2 + y3
  
  theta <- theta0
  
  for (iter in 1:maxit) {
    theta.old <- theta
    
    # E-step
    m <- y1 * theta.old / (1 + theta.old)
    
    # M-step
    theta <- (m + y4) / (m + y4 + A)
    
    if (abs(theta - theta.old) < tol) break
  }
  
  # Louis observed information
  q <- theta / (1 + theta)
  m <- y1 * q
  v <- y1 * q * (1 - q)
  
  J <- (m + y4) / theta^2 + A / (1 - theta)^2 - v / theta^2
  V <- 1 / J
  se <- sqrt(V)
  
  list(theta = theta, info = J, V = V, se = se, iter = iter)
}

y <- c(108, 31, 27, 34)
em.fit(y)
```

```r
$V

$se
[1] 0.04721044
```

# (v) Simulation study

A reasonable simulation design is:

1. Fix \(n=200\).
2. Choose an interior true value, say \(\theta_0=0.5\).
3. Simulate many datasets \(Y^{(b)}\sim\text{Multinomial}(200;p(\theta_0))\).
4. For each dataset compute \(\hat\theta^{(b)}\) and \(\hat V^{(b)}\).
5. Check:
   - Normality of
     \[
     Z_b
     =
     \frac{\hat\theta^{(b)}-\theta_0}{\sqrt{\hat V^{(b)}}}.
     \]
   - Agreement between
     \[
     \operatorname{Var}_{\text{MC}}(\hat\theta)
     \]
     and
     \[
     \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \hat V^{(b)}.
     \]

R code:

```r
mle.closed <- function(Y) {
  n <- rowSums(Y)
  A <- Y[, 2] + Y[, 3]
  D <- Y[, 1] - A
  y4 <- Y[, 4]
  
  theta.hat <- (D + sqrt(D^2 + 4 * n * y4)) / (2 * n)
  theta.hat
}

obs.info <- function(Y, theta.hat) {
  y1 <- Y[, 1]
  A  <- Y[, 2] + Y[, 3]
  y4 <- Y[, 4]
  
  y1 / (1 + theta.hat)^2 +
    A / (1 - theta.hat)^2 +
    y4 / theta.hat^2
}

sim.check <- function(theta0 = 0.5, n = 200, B = 50000, seed = 123) {
  set.seed(seed)
  
  p <- c((1 + theta0) / 3,
         (1 - theta0) / 3,
         (1 - theta0) / 3,
         theta0 / 3)
  
  Y <- t(rmultinom(B, n, p))
  
  theta.hat <- mle.closed(Y)
  J.hat <- obs.info(Y, theta.hat)
  V.hat <- 1 / J.hat
  se.hat <- sqrt(V.hat)
  
  Z <- (theta.hat - theta0) / se.hat
  
  out <- c(
    mean.theta.hat = mean(theta.hat),
    bias = mean(theta.hat) - theta0,
    empirical.sd = sd(theta.hat),
    mean.SE = mean(se.hat),
    sqrt.mean.Vhat = sqrt(mean(V.hat)),
    var.ratio = var(theta.hat) / mean(V.hat),
    coverage.95 = mean(abs(theta.hat - theta0) <= 1.96 * se.hat),
    mean.Z = mean(Z),
    sd.Z = sd(Z),
    q025.Z = quantile(Z, 0.025),
    q500.Z = quantile(Z, 0.500),
    q975.Z = quantile(Z, 0.975)
  )
  
  print(out)
  
  hist(Z, probability = TRUE, breaks = 50,
       main = "Studentized MLE",
       xlab = expression((hat(theta) - theta[0]) / sqrt(hat(V))))
  curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, col = 2, lwd = 2)
  
  qqnorm(Z)
  qqline(Z, col = 2, lwd = 2)
  
  invisible(out)
}

sim.check(theta0 = 0.5, n = 200, B = 50000)
```

```r
mean.SE          ≈ 0.047
sqrt.mean.Vhat   ≈ 0.047
var.ratio        ≈ 1.00

mean.Z           ≈ 0
sd.Z             ≈ 1

q500.Z           ≈ 0
q975.Z           ≈ 1.96
```

being close to \(1\) confirms that \(\hat V\) is a good estimator of the variance of \(\hat\theta\) at \(n=200\).
